case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a free, advertising-supported sports website that provides short video clips qualifies as a “video tape service provider” and/or whether its users qualify as “consumers” under the Video Privacy Protection Act such that alleged sharing of viewing information triggers VPPA liability.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 2710 (the Video Privacy Protection Act of 1988), including the definitions in § 2710(a) (e.g., “consumer,” “video tape service provider,” and “personally identifiable information”) and the disclosure prohibition in § 2710(b)(1).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Salazar argues the Sixth Circuit adopted an unduly narrow, textually unsound interpretation of the VPPA that effectively limits the statute to legacy video-rental-type businesses; he contends modern online publishers that deliver video content (including free clips) can be covered “video tape service providers,” and that his interaction with 247Sports makes him a protected “consumer,” so the court should resolve the circuit split and reverse on the statutory-interpretation question (and he stresses this case is a clean vehicle with a final judgment, unlike the related NBA petition).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Paramount/247Sports argues certiorari should be denied because the case is a poor vehicle and Salazar loses as a matter of law even if the Court reached the “consumer” question; it maintains 247Sports is a sports news website (not a business that rents/sells/subscribes to audiovisual works) and that the VPPA’s text and purpose do not extend to free online news clips, and it further emphasizes that multiple other issues (including separate circuit splits over VPPA elements like “personally identifiable information” standards and standing/percolation concerns) counsel against Supreme Court review now.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that “delivery” is not, by its terms, limited to pay-per-view or Blockbuster-style rentals, and the VPPA can reach modern modes of transmission. But the Act’s enacted text links liability to a particular relationship: a covered plaintiff must be a “consumer” defined as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber,” and §2710(b)(1) authorizes suit only by a “consumer of such provider,” reinforcing (as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan note) a provider–customer connection rather than a casual website visit. Reading “delivery” to cover any ad-supported publisher that incidentally streams clips would drain “engaged in the business” and the transactional terms Congress chose of limiting force, effectively converting this targeted statute into a general web-tracking law. On these pleadings, the site’s principal business and the user’s relationship do not plausibly fit the statute’s paired definitions, so dismissal is proper and any broader modernization is for Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that we should not smuggle a payment requirement into “delivery,” and digital transmission can qualify as delivery in an appropriate case. But Chief Justice Roberts correctly emphasizes the statute’s linked definitions and §2710(b)(1)’s limitation to a “consumer of such provider,” which presupposes the renter/purchaser/subscriber relationship Congress chose to define. Reading “delivery” untethered from “engaged in the business” and the company it keeps with “rental” and “sale,” as Justice Barrett notes, would effectively convert the VPPA into a general web-tracking regime whenever a publisher embeds clips. On these pleadings—a free, ad-supported sports news site with clips incidental to journalism—the statutory predicates are missing, and any broader modernization must come from Congress rather than judicial reconstruction of the definitional scheme.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that “delivery” need not entail payment and can include modern digital transmission, but her approach, on this record, risks collapsing the VPPA’s limiting definitions into a boundless “any website with video” rule. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, §2710’s structure links a covered defendant to a covered plaintiff through a defined, transactional relationship—suit lies only by a “consumer of such provider,” and “consumer” is limited to a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber,” terms that are not plausibly satisfied by a casual viewer of free, ad-supported clips on a broader news site. Absent concrete allegations showing that this entity is actually “engaged in the business” of delivering audiovisual materials as the product (rather than an incidental feature) and that the plaintiff is a “subscriber” in something like the statutory sense, extending coverage would require speculation about applications. I would affirm while leaving open that a different platform or a better-developed record showing a subscription-like relationship could present a different case.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s whole-statute argument—especially the “consumer of such provider” linkage in §2710(b)(1)—is the most serious constraint, and I agree it requires some provider–consumer relationship beyond a one-off, drive-by page view. But that structural point does not justify importing a payment requirement the text never states, nor does it warrant treating “delivery” as limited to rental/sale-like transactions when Congress separately listed “delivery” alongside those terms. Justice Barrett’s noscitur concern about collapsing the Act into “any website with video” is real, yet it is addressed by a function-and-context inquiry into whether the defendant is plausibly “engaged in the business … of … delivery” and whether the plaintiff plausibly qualifies as a “subscriber” on the pleadings, rather than by categorically excluding ad-supported services at Rule 12. On this record, the Sixth Circuit’s narrowing reads modern ongoing user relationships out of “subscriber” and improperly resolves factual and contextual questions about the service’s business model and the user’s relationship at the threshold.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that we should not freeze the VPPA in 1988 technology, and “delivery” can naturally include digital transmission. But the statute does not regulate delivery in the abstract: it limits covered defendants to those “engaged in the business” of rental, sale, or delivery, and it limits plaintiffs to “consumers” defined as “renter[s], purchaser[s], or subscriber[s],” with §2710(b)(1)’s “consumer of such provider” linking the two, as the Chief Justice stresses. Reading “delivery” to cover any ad-supported publisher that incidentally streams clips would erase those limiting words and effectively convert the VPPA into a general web-tracking law—an expansion better left to Congress. On these pleadings, I do not see the requisite provider–consumer relationship or a video-delivery business, so I would affirm dismissal while leaving room for a different record involving a video-centric service or a true subscription relationship (Justice Alito’s point).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that the VPPA’s text does not impose a “for a fee” requirement, and we should not add one. But her approach still risks untethering “delivery” from the limiting words Congress did enact—“engaged in the business” and the company it keeps with “rental” and “sale”—and thereby turning the definition into an atextual “any website with video” rule. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the statute’s linked definitions and §2710(b)(1)’s authorization of suit only by a “consumer of such provider” presuppose a renter/purchaser/subscriber relationship with a provider engaged in that business, which is not plausibly alleged by a casual, free viewing of embedded clips on a sports news site. If Congress wishes to extend this targeted statute into a general regime for digital tracking disclosures, it may do so, but we should not revise the statutory predicates to get there.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that “delivery” in § 2710(a)(4) can naturally encompass modern digital transmission and need not be limited to paid Blockbuster-style transactions. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, the enacted definitions operate as a linked scheme: liability runs only to a “consumer of such provider,” and “consumer” is limited to a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber,” which in context connotes a provider-customer relationship rather than a casual visit to a free, ad-supported news site with incidental clips. Reading “delivery” alone to cover any website that transmits video would drain “engaged in the business” of meaning and effectively convert the VPPA into a general web-tracking statute—an expansion not supported by the text and better left to Congress. Even if third-party pixel disclosure could present concreteness under TransUnion, the statutory-coverage defect is dispositive on these pleaded facts.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that “delivery” can include free, ad-supported distribution and that we should not freeze the VPPA in 1988 technology. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that the statute’s definitions are linked: suit lies only for a “consumer of such provider,” and “consumer” is limited to a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber,” which in ordinary usage connotes an ongoing, affirmative relationship with the provider—something more than a casual visit to a news site with embedded clips. Reading “delivery” untethered from “engaged in the business” and from its statutory neighbors (“rental” and “sale”) risks collapsing “video tape service provider” into “any website with video,” effectively converting a targeted privacy statute into an omnibus web-tracking law. On these pleadings, I would affirm, while leaving open (as Justice Alito notes) that a different record involving a video-centric service or a bona fide subscription relationship could present a different case.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to resist importing a fee-for-service requirement the VPPA does not state, and to note that “delivery” can encompass modern digital distribution. But at the right level of specificity, that functional framing risks collapsing the statute’s limiting touchstones—“engaged in the business” and the paired “consumer of such provider” requirement—into an atextual “has video” rule that would sweep in ordinary online publishers. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, § 2710(b)(1)’s “consumer of such provider” links the definitions and presupposes a renter/purchaser/subscriber relationship with a covered provider; on these pleadings, a free, ad-supported sports journalism site with incidental clips and a casual viewer does not plausibly satisfy those linked predicates. Given the chilling risk of uncertain liability for commonplace analytics and embedded media, I would affirm and leave any modernization of this targeted statute to Congress.

John Roberts.reasoning: The VPPA’s operative text pairs a “consumer” (a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber”) with a “video tape service provider” (one “engaged in the business … of rental, sale or delivery of … audio visual materials”), and § 2710(b)(1) authorizes suit only by a “consumer of such provider,” confirming the definitions work together rather than extending to any website visitor. Read in that whole-statute context, a free, advertising-supported sports news site that merely makes short clips available without any rental, sale, or subscription relationship is not “engaged in the business” of rental or sale, and the petitioner’s casual use of clips does not make him a “renter” or “purchaser,” nor a “subscriber” in the statutory sense. The continuity of the enacted 1988 language—focused on transactional relationships for “rental, sale or delivery” of prerecorded audiovisual materials—counsels against stretching the definition to cover every ad-supported publisher that streams clips. On these facts, petitioner falls outside the statute’s defined plaintiff class, so the alleged disclosure does not trigger VPPA liability.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The VPPA’s text and structure define a “video tape service provider” as a person “engaged in the business” of “rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials,” and a “consumer” as one who is a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber” of such goods or services. Read in that statutory setting—and against the specific problem Congress targeted in 1988 (commercial video-rental disclosure, not general online publishing)—a free, advertising-supported sports news site offering short clips looks more like a publisher that incidentally hosts video than a business whose relevant transaction is renting/selling/subscribing to audiovisual materials. The modern platform realities Salazar highlights (ad monetization, tracking pixels, algorithmic distribution) may show how disclosure happens at scale, but they do not supply the missing statutory predicates of a qualifying “provider” and “consumer” relationship grounded in rental/purchase/subscription. Given that extension to free news clips would effectively convert much of the ad-supported web into VPPA-regulated “video tape service” absent clear textual direction, I would affirm dismissal and leave any modernization to Congress.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: On this record, I would not extend the VPPA to a free, advertising-supported sports news site that offers short clips absent a concrete, non-speculative showing that the site’s business is “engaged in the rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials” in the sense Congress targeted, rather than merely publishing incidental video as part of a broader news product. Petitioner’s theory risks treating any multipurpose website with embedded video as a “video tape service provider,” but the statute’s defined categories require a function-specific, evidence-based inquiry into what 247Sports actually delivers, how users access it, and whether the user relationship resembles the statute’s paradigmatic “rental/sale/subscription” transaction—issues that cannot be resolved by broad characterization alone. Likewise, without a developed showing that petitioner was a “consumer” (as renter, purchaser, or subscriber) rather than a casual visitor, imposing VPPA liability would rest on speculation about statutory coverage. Given that mismatch between the statute’s operative thresholds/definitions and the site’s described business model, I would affirm the judgment for respondent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Sixth Circuit’s reading effectively narrows the VPPA to legacy video-rental analogs, but the statutory definitions direct us to classify coverage by what the entity does—whether it is “engaged in the business . . . of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials”—not by whether it charges a subscription or looks like Blockbuster. On Salazar’s allegations, 247Sports systematically delivers identifiable video clips to users as part of its business model, and denying coverage solely because the clips are free or embedded in an advertising-supported publisher would elevate form over the statute’s text and purpose, undermining Congress’s privacy-protective scheme. Likewise, treating users as non-“consumers” absent payment or formal subscription would create an atextual carveout where modern digital “delivery” is most prevalent, even though the complaint plausibly alleges an ongoing user relationship tied to viewing specific videos. At minimum, the better reading is that the VPPA’s protection turns on the delivery of audiovisual materials and the user’s receipt/request of them, so dismissal at the pleading stage was unwarranted.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Start with the statute’s text. A “video tape service provider” is a person “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials,” and a “consumer” is a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber” of such goods or services. On these facts, 247Sports is primarily a sports news site offering short, free, ad-supported clips as an adjunct to written reporting, so characterizing it as being in the ‘business’ of delivering audiovisual materials in the sense the VPPA uses that term stretches the ordinary meaning and statutory structure beyond its rental/sale/subscription hooks; and Salazar’s use—without payment or any ongoing subscription-like commitment—does not fit the statute’s renter/purchaser/subscriber categories. Whatever the privacy risks of pixel-based tracking and downstream disclosure (sale, hacking, subpoena), the Court’s role here is to apply Congress’s chosen definitions, and this record does not place 247Sports (or Salazar) on the covered side of those definitional lines.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Start with the statute’s text. The VPPA defines a “video tape service provider” as a person “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials,” and the most natural reading of “engaged in the business” plus the specific nouns (“rental, sale”) suggests a commercial video-content enterprise rather than a general sports-news website that merely embeds short, advertising-supported clips ancillary to its journalism. On these alleged facts, extending the Act to any ad-supported publisher that happens to “deliver” some videos would treat an incidental feature as the business itself and would effectively erase the limiting words Congress chose, converting “video tape service provider” into “any website with video,” a step the text does not warrant. Absent a clearer statutory basis, policy arguments about updating an older statute for modern media belong to Congress, and the narrower construction best honors the enacted definitions without judicially rewriting their limits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Starting with the enacted text, a free, advertising-supported sports news site offering incidental short clips is not, in ordinary statutory usage, a “video tape service provider” that is “engaged in the business” of rental, sale, or delivery of “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials” in the way the VPPA contemplates; stretching those words to cover a general-interest publisher would effectively expand the statute beyond its meaning rather than apply it to new technology. For the same reason, a visitor who merely watches free clips without an ongoing relationship resembling renting, purchasing, or subscribing does not naturally fit the statute’s “consumer” definition, which presupposes a provider-consumer transactional relationship. Even assuming a disclosure to a third party (e.g., Facebook via a pixel) could satisfy concreteness under TransUnion, the threshold statutory-coverage problem remains dispositive on these facts, so the complaint fails as a matter of law. The proper course is to apply the line Congress drew in the statute’s operative definitions and leave any broader regulation of online tracking to Congress.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Starting with the text and its original public meaning, § 2710(a)(4) defines a “video tape service provider” as a person “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials,” and the best reading of “engaged in the business” plus the enumerated commercial modes (rental, sale, subscription-like delivery) points to an enterprise whose business is furnishing audiovisual works—not a general sports-news site that incidentally embeds free, advertising-supported clips. Reading “delivery” in light of its neighbors (noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis) avoids converting the VPPA into a sweeping online-tracking statute for any webpage that transmits video, a result hard to square with the statute’s targeted response to the Bork video-rental disclosures. Even if a user could be a “consumer” when she becomes a “subscriber” (§ 2710(a)(1)), Salazar’s alleged conduct here (watching short clips on a free site without a qualifying subscription relationship) does not fit that term’s ordinary meaning in this statutory context. Precedent counsels restraint in expanding criminal/penal-style privacy statutes beyond their text, consistent with this Court’s approach to overbroad readings in Yates and Fischer.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: At the right level of specificity, the function at issue is a free, advertising-supported sports news website that incidentally provides short clips to complement reporting—not a provider whose business is renting, selling, or delivering video materials as the relevant product. Faithfully applying the VPPA’s definitional touchstones, 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a) ties “video tape service provider” to being “engaged in the business” of providing “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials,” and treating any clip-hosting publisher as covered would collapse that inquiry into a broad, category-level “has video” test the statute does not support. That same specificity concern carries to “consumer”: on these facts, the alleged interaction with 247Sports is best characterized as consuming news content, not establishing the kind of rental/purchase/subscription relationship the Act targets. Given the statute’s text-driven limits and the real-world chilling risk that an overbroad reading would create for online journalism and ordinary web analytics absent clearer congressional direction, I would affirm.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a free, ad-supported sports news website that publishes video clips is a “video tape service provider” under the Video Privacy Protection Act such that it can be liable for disclosing user viewing information.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Video Privacy Protection Act (VPPA), 18 U.S.C. § 2710 (including definitions in § 2710(a) and the disclosure prohibition in § 2710(b)(1)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Salazar argues the Sixth Circuit adopted an unduly narrow, textually misguided interpretation of the VPPA by effectively limiting the statute to businesses akin to traditional video rental/sales operations; he contends that modern digital publishers that deliver video content (including via websites with clips) can fall within the VPPA’s scope, and that Supreme Court review is warranted to resolve an acknowledged circuit split on the VPPA’s reach (also implicated in the NBA-related petition) using this case as a clean vehicle because it comes to the Court after a final judgment and without the procedural complications present in the other petition.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Paramount/247Sports argues certiorari should be denied because the case is a poor vehicle and/or the petition fails on the merits: 247Sports is fundamentally a free sports news site—not a business that rents, sells, or offers subscriptions to video content—so the VPPA (enacted to address disclosure of video rental records) does not cover it; respondent further contends Salazar’s complaint fails for multiple independent reasons (not just the “consumer”/coverage question), and emphasizes that the Court should allow issues to continue percolating rather than taking up a case where dispositive problems would prevent clean resolution of the presented question.

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point is that “delivery” of “similar audio visual materials” can naturally encompass internet streaming, and we should not freeze the VPPA in a VHS-era marketplace. But, as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, the definition turns on being “engaged in the business” of renting, selling, or delivering those materials, and that limiting language—together with the statute’s linkage of “consumer” to a renter/purchaser/subscriber relationship with “such provider”—does real work that petitioner’s reading largely erases. Justice Thomas’s ejusdem generis point further supports reading “similar” as tethered to an enterprise centered on furnishing discrete audiovisual works, not general news publishing with incidental clips. A narrow, facts-bound holding that respondent’s alleged core business is journalism supported by advertising and that any video delivery is ancillary resolves this case without opining on entities whose primary product is video delivery.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point is that “delivery” of “similar audio visual materials” can naturally encompass streaming video given how thoroughly internet video has displaced the VHS-era market Congress confronted. But, as Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice stress, the statute does not regulate every entity that can transmit video; it regulates those “engaged in the business” of renting, selling, or delivering such materials, and that limiting phrase must constrain the definition rather than be read out of it. Reading “delivery” to reach an ad-supported news publisher that incidentally embeds clips would sever the definition from the statute’s structure—especially the “consumer” relationship (renter/purchaser/subscriber) tied to “such provider”—and effectively convert a targeted privacy rule into a sweeping regime for ordinary web analytics. On the pleaded facts, 247Sports’ core business is publishing journalism supported by ads, with video ancillary, so it is not a §2710(a)(4) provider here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains that "delivery" of "similar audio visual materials" can naturally describe streaming or embedded clips, so the definition could be read with technological neutrality. But, as Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice stress, that reading cannot be severed from the statute’s limiting phrase "engaged in the business" and the definition of "consumer" as a renter/purchaser/subscriber of "such provider," which presuppose a commercial relationship centered on furnishing audiovisual materials as the product. On this record, treating an ad-supported news publisher with incidental video as a covered "video tape service provider" would drain those limiting words of meaning and effectively convert a targeted privacy statute into a broad regulation of ordinary web publishing and analytics without a clear textual anchor. Consistent with a cautious, record-based approach to statutory reach, this case is a poor vehicle for adopting petitioner’s expansive construction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point remains that “delivery” of “similar audio visual materials” can naturally encompass streaming video, and I do not discount Congress’s use of technology-flexible language. But, as Justice Barrett explains, the statute’s definitional structure links “consumer” (a renter/purchaser/subscriber) to “such provider,” which presupposes a provider-consumer relationship in which furnishing audiovisual materials is the business—not incidental clip delivery by an ad-supported news publisher. As the Chief notes, reading “engaged in the business” to sweep in any site that serves video would effectively erase that limiting phrase and predictably expand the VPPA into routine web-analytics disclosures across digital journalism, with significant chilling consequences absent a clear congressional choice. On the pleaded facts, 247Sports is not plausibly a §2710(a)(4) “video tape service provider,” so the VPPA claim fails at the threshold.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point is that “delivery” of “similar audio visual materials” can naturally encompass online streaming, so the VPPA should not be frozen in a VHS era. But as Justice Barrett stresses, §2710(a)(4) does not just ask whether a defendant can transmit video; it asks whether the defendant is “engaged in the business” of renting, selling, or delivering those materials—limiting language that must be given effect, especially in a statute built around a renter/purchaser/subscriber relationship. On the pleaded facts, 247Sports functions as an ad-supported news publisher that may embed clips incidentally, not an enterprise whose commercial offering is furnishing discrete audiovisual works to consumers in the way the definition contemplates. As the Chief Justice warns, adopting petitioner’s reading would effectively erase “engaged in the business” and transform a targeted privacy statute into a broad regulation of ordinary web publishing and analytics without clear textual authorization.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point is that “delivery” and “similar audio visual materials” are naturally capacious enough to reach streaming clips, and Congress needn’t name the Internet to regulate it. But, as Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice stress, the definition does not stop at “delivery”; it covers only an entity “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery” of those materials, and that limiting phrase must be given operative effect. Reading it to encompass any ad-supported publisher that incidentally transmits video would drain the limitation of meaning and sit uneasily with the statute’s structural linkage of “consumer” (a renter, purchaser, or subscriber) to “such provider.” On the pleaded facts, respondent looks like a news publisher with ancillary clips, not a business whose product is furnishing audiovisual materials in the statutory sense, so §2710(a)(4) does not reach it.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point is that “delivery” of “similar audio visual materials” can naturally include online transmission of video clips, so a technologically updated reading could bring respondent within the statute. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, that reading risks draining the limiting phrase “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery” of operative force and disconnecting the definition of “consumer” (a renter/purchaser/subscriber) from “such provider,” which presupposes a commercial relationship centered on furnishing audiovisual materials as the product. Justice Thomas’s ejusdem generis point further supports reading “similar” in light of the VHS-era paradigm Congress targeted, not as a general hook to federalize routine web publishing and analytics whenever a site embeds incidental video. On the pleadings here—where the core enterprise is ad-supported journalism with ancillary clips—the complaint does not plausibly allege respondent is a “video tape service provider” under §2710(a)(4).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point is that “delivery” and “similar audio visual materials” can linguistically encompass streaming clips, so an ad-supported publisher “delivers” video. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice stress, that reading cannot be severed from the limiting phrase “engaged in the business” and the statute’s definitional linkage of “consumer” (a renter, purchaser, or subscriber) to “such provider,” which presupposes a commercial relationship centered on furnishing audiovisual materials as the product. Justice Thomas’s noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis point further confirms that “similar” is tethered to the kind of discrete audiovisual-offerings business Congress described, not generalized journalism with incidental clips. The breadth consequences are thus confirmatory: if petitioner’s construction is right, the limiting words do little work and the VPPA becomes a sweeping web-analytics regime without clear textual warrant.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains that “delivery” of “similar audio visual materials” can naturally encompass online streaming, and Congress need not employ “magic words” to account for new technology. But, as Justice Barrett explains, the definitional structure—linking a “video tape service provider” to being “engaged in the business” and tying “consumer” to a renter/purchaser/subscriber relationship with “such provider”—signals the right level of specificity: a transactional, video-service line of business, not general web publishing with incidental clips. Chief Justice Roberts’s concern about effectively federalizing routine journalism/analytics underscores how petitioner’s reading would drain “engaged in the business” of limiting force, contrary to our ordinary textual approach. Statutory history confirming Congress’s focus on video rental records corroborates that, on these pleaded facts, respondent is not plausibly a covered provider under §2710(a)(4).

John Roberts.reasoning: The VPPA’s text targets entities “engaged in the business” of renting, selling, or delivering “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” which naturally denotes a business whose product is the provision of video content—not a free, ad-supported sports-news website for which video clips are ancillary to written reporting. Reading “similar audio visual materials” to include any online video clip would sever the definition from its limiting “engaged in the business” language and effectively federalize routine web analytics on sites that are not video-delivery businesses. On these facts, 247Sports functions primarily as a news publisher; treating it as a “video tape service provider” would expand the statute beyond the kind of video-service relationship Congress addressed. The complaint therefore fails at the coverage element: respondent is not the type of provider the VPPA regulates.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The VPPA’s text, read in statutory context, defines a “video tape service provider” as one “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery” of “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” which—under noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis—targets providers whose business model centers on furnishing discrete video materials or services, not a free, ad-supported news site where video clips are ancillary to written reporting. Technological change matters, but it does not license rewriting the statute’s targeted coverage from the video-rental/paid-delivery paradigm Congress addressed into a sweeping rule for any ad-monetized website that happens to “deliver” clips over the internet. Structurally, extending VPPA liability to general publishers would transform a focused privacy regime into a broad prohibition affecting vast, algorithmically distributed and ad-supported online content at modern scale—an expansion Congress has not clearly enacted. Because 247Sports’ core business is sports news content supported by advertising rather than renting, selling, or subscription-delivering audiovisual materials, it falls outside §2710(a)(4).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The statutory question turns on the VPPA’s defined terms and real-world coverage, and on this record 247Sports is fundamentally a free, ad-supported sports news website whose video clips are ancillary to its journalism—not a business that “rents, sells, or delivers” audiovisual materials in the way the statute’s text and structure contemplate. Absent concrete allegations that 247Sports’ enterprise is the delivery of video content (as opposed to primarily non-expressive news publishing with incidental video), extending “video tape service provider” to it risks converting a technology-specific privacy statute into a sweeping regulation of ordinary digital publishers without a clear textual anchor. A cautious, record-based approach counsels against adopting petitioner’s broad construction in a case that (by respondent’s account) presents multiple independent pleading defects, making it a poor vehicle for announcing an expansive interpretation. Consistent with the Court’s admonitions against overreading older, technology-focused statutes beyond their defined terms and context, the better reading is that this site is outside the VPPA’s core reach.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Applying a context- and effects-sensitive approach, I would read “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery” to require that delivering audiovisual materials be a meaningful part of the enterprise’s commercial offering, not merely incidental to operating a free, ad-supported sports news site. On these facts, the website’s core function is publishing journalism and monetizing attention through advertising; treating every publisher that embeds clips as a “video tape service provider” would sweep broadly in ways Congress did not clearly choose and could predictably chill digital newsgathering and consumption by attaching statutory damages to routine analytics and ad-tech disclosures. That breadth is especially concerning where the statute’s trigger would turn on the content-format consumed (video versus text), a mismatch with the VPPA’s historical focus on transactional video services and the “breathing space” privacy interests it sought to protect without overdeterring speech-adjacent activity. Because this case is a poor fit for extending the VPPA beyond businesses that actually trade in video delivery as a product, I would affirm the narrower interpretation here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Start with the VPPA’s text: it reaches only a person “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials.” A free, ad-supported sports news site that primarily publishes provider-preselected articles and embeds short clips looks, in ordinary terms and functional operation, like a digital publisher using video as an incidental feature of its journalism—not a business whose product is the delivery of “similar audio visual materials” in the way the statute contemplates. Reading “engaged in the business” to cover any website that happens to deliver some videos would erase the limiting work done by that phrase and by “similar,” effectively converting a targeted privacy statute for video-distribution businesses into a sweeping regulation of general news sites. On these facts, 247Sports is better characterized as a news outlet than a video-delivery service, so it falls outside § 2710(a)(4).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The VPPA’s text covers only a “person engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials.” A free, ad-supported sports news site whose principal business is publishing news—while incidentally hosting short video clips—does not naturally fit that enacted description, and nothing in the statute’s ordinary terms extends it to any website that merely “delivers” some video as an adjunct to a different business. Petitioner’s broader, policy-driven reading would require us to move away from the statute’s limiting words (“engaged in the business” and “similar audio visual materials”) and treat them as surplusage. Applying the text as written to these facts, 247Sports is not a covered “video tape service provider,” so it cannot incur VPPA liability on this theory.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The precise interpretive inquiry is what Congress meant by “video tape service provider,” defined as a person “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials.” Read in text-and-structure context—especially the modifiers “engaged in the business” and “similar” tied to “prerecorded video cassette tapes”—a free, ad-supported sports news website that merely posts clips as part of a broader publishing enterprise is not plausibly in the business of renting, selling, or delivering video materials in the VPPA sense. The statute’s enacted purpose—responding to disclosure of video rental records—confirms that Congress targeted businesses whose commercial relationship with consumers is centered on providing video materials, not general-content websites incidentally offering videos funded by advertising. Even assuming a cause of action, the Court should be wary of stretching a 1988 privacy statute beyond its defined terms to regulate modern web analytics where the complained-of disclosure is not tied to a qualifying provider-consumer video transaction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Start with the VPPA’s text and structure: §2710(b)(1) bars disclosure of information identifying a “consumer,” and the paired definitions in §2710(a) link “consumer” (a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber”) to “such provider,” i.e., an entity “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery” of covered audiovisual materials. Reading those definitions together, a free, ad-supported sports news website that merely publishes clips is not plausibly “engaged in the business” of renting, selling, or delivering audiovisual materials in the sense the statute uses—its business is journalism/advertising, and any video “delivery” is incidental to that enterprise rather than the covered line of business. The alternative reading would expand a statute aimed at video rental records to sweep in ordinary web publishers that embed or host clips and use commonplace analytics/advertising tools, an overbroad regime that the enacted text does not clearly adopt; neither enforcement discretion nor mens rea supplies a textual limiting principle. That consequence serves as confirmatory “extra icing,” but the decisive point remains the statute’s definitional context and internal pairing of “consumer” with providers in the rental/sale/delivery business.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying the VPPA’s text at the right level of specificity, the operative question is whether 247Sports’ particular activity—operating a free, ad-supported sports news site that incidentally “publishes video clips”—amounts to “rent[ing], sell[ing], or deliver[ing] prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials” “as a regular part of its business” under § 2710(a)(4), rather than whether the company is broadly in the “video” business. Read naturally, and in light of the statute’s history targeting disclosure of video rental records, that definition most comfortably fits entities whose business is to provide audiovisual materials as a core offering to consumers, not a general news publisher whose principal product is journalism supported by advertising. Congress need not use magic words to regulate new technologies, but the clear-notice principle still counsels against stretching “video tape service provider” beyond its functionally video-distribution-centered lane absent clearer textual direction that Congress meant to sweep in free, ad-driven publishers merely because they embed clips. On that activity-focused, text-and-context reading, 247Sports is not plausibly a “video tape service provider” on these facts, so dismissal is appropriate.
